paragraphs.text: Combined Cycle Gas Turbine power stations have long relied on process modelling for design and development, and the practice now extends over the whole plant lifecycle: early concept testing, design, development and operation. During operation a model can be applied offline, meaning it is solved separately from the plant, typically to optimise operation or to assess plant modifications. It can also be applied online, running alongside the real plant and fed with measured data from the plant information system; in that role it supports performance monitoring, tracking of equipment degradation and maintenance scheduling, while its estimates can reconcile sensor readings, add knowledge about the plant and help troubleshooting.

A CCGT station couples a gas turbine to a steam cycle through a heat recovery steam generator (HRSG), which takes heat from the gas turbine exhaust to boil water for the steam cycle by means of a series of heat exchangers. Because these heat exchangers are central to the station, the performance and accuracy of their models within the process model matter most. The literature review found two rival ways of modelling how the overall heat transfer coefficient varies: semi-empirical correlations built for a particular heat transfer problem, or multiplying a nominal value (normally the design overall heat transfer coefficient) by weights built from how design-condition fluid properties compare with those at the conditions of interest, each ratio taken to a constant exponent chosen for the problem. A third option is to treat the overall heat transfer coefficient as essentially unchanged from design and hold it constant.

These three ways of estimating the overall heat transfer coefficient correspond to three levels of modelling fidelity. Each was built into a heat exchanger model, named the Correlation, Weighted and Basic heat exchangers, and these were placed in a model of the HRSG at the Otahuhu B CCGT power station in Auckland, New Zealand. The HRSG was simulated at four load points covering the plant operating range and the results were compared with measured plant data. The Weighted model tracked the load-driven changes in real heat exchanger behaviour most accurately. The Correlation model reproduced the trends in the plant data but was frequently offset because its initial overall heat transfer coefficient estimate was inaccurate. The Basic model was least accurate and could not follow the trends as load changed. The Correlation model also generally took more than ten times as long to solve as the other two models.

Numerical models of industrial processes are an important aid for both designing and running thermal power plants. At the design stage they help size equipment, check whether alternative configurations can meet the specification, and confirm by simulation across the operating range that the plant behaves as intended off-design. For existing plants, simulation results serve many analyses, such as finding optimal operating parameters under varying conditions or plant monitoring, where a departure of measured behaviour from model predictions can reveal degraded or malfunctioning equipment and so guide maintenance scheduling. Heat exchanger modelling is well established in the literature, yet even for steady-state simulation several modelling methodologies remain in use in published work and in commercial software.

The study concerns the Otahuhu B combined cycle gas turbine (CCGT) power station run by Contact Energy Ltd. in Auckland, New Zealand. Sensors report the plant state to controllers, to operators through the Human Machine Interface (HMI), and to the plant PI Historian database for later review. Cost and measurement difficulty restrict the number and type of sensors, particularly for temperatures inside the heat recovery steam generator (HRSG), where only a few points are measured routinely. One remedy is a real-time simulation mirroring the plant: once validated against available measurements, it can estimate the missing temperatures and help reconcile faulty sensor readings, which requires models that accurately predict how the individual heat exchangers perform. A footnote states that Otahuhu B has since been decommissioned, and that all plant information and operating data used were gathered beforehand.

To identify the best approach, the work builds heat exchanger models that implement these different methods, embeds them in a steady-state Otahuhu B HRSG model, validates the results against real operating data and compares how each heat exchanger model performs. The chapter goes on to give a general overview of CCGT operation, then focuses on Otahuhu B, describes the heat exchangers in its HRSG and the modelling framework, and finally states the research aims and outlines the rest of the thesis.

Combined Cycle Gas Turbines (CCGT) are presently the most efficient fossil-fuelled thermal power plants; Figure 1.1 gives the process flow of a single pressure level CCGT station. Two cycles operate together. The gas turbine follows the Brayton cycle: compressed air enters the combustion chamber, is mixed with natural gas and burned, and the hot exhaust expands through the turbine to produce work that drives both the compressor and an electrical generator. Exhaust leaving the turbine is still above 500 °C, so further energy is recovered in a second stage running on the standard Rankine cycle by passing the exhaust through the Heat Recovery Steam Generator (HRSG).

The HRSG is in essence a large duct holding many heat exchangers, through which exhaust heat is taken up to turn high-pressure water inside the heat exchanger coils into superheated steam. This steam expands through steam turbines to produce more work and electricity, is then condensed to water and pumped back to high pressure to close the cycle. Modern CCGT stations can exceed 60 % efficiency, against roughly 40 % for single cycle plants [68, 41, 55].
Figure 1.1 caption: process flow diagram of a single pressure level combined cycle gas turbine power station (printed as "Combine cycle").

The 400 MW Otahuhu B CCGT station in Auckland, New Zealand, run by Contact Energy Ltd., is built around one Siemens SGT5-4000F V94.3A(2) gas turbine rated at 288 MW and a three pressure level HRSG with reheat. Its steam drives low, intermediate and high pressure turbines (LP, IP and HP); the HP turbine exhaust is combined with IP steam before the reheater. A deaerator for removing entrained gases from the circulating water sits after the condensate preheater but runs only intermittently, since the condenser also deaerates. Steam leaving the LP turbine, still of high quality, is condensed to liquid in a condenser cooled with water drawn from the local estuary, and that water is itself cooled in an 8-cell evaporative, hybrid cooling tower.

The HRSG (written "heat recovery stream generator" in the original) is a large duct housing the heat exchangers of every steam pressure level. Within one pressure level, heat exchangers fall into three groups according to the water/steam phase they handle. The economiser preheats feed water to about 6 − 17 °C below saturation [37], this margin being the approach point temperature difference ∆Tapp. The evaporator then boils the water; the gap between the exhaust gas temperature leaving the evaporator and the saturation temperature is the pinch point temperature difference ∆Tpinch, typically 17−33 °C at design [37]. The superheater finally raises the steam to the required outlet temperature. ∆Tapp and ∆Tpinch are key HRSG design quantities: lower values improve thermal efficiency but demand more heat exchanger surface area, with correspondingly greater size and cost.

Economiser and superheater duties may each be split over several heat exchangers, which, together with those of any other pressure levels, are placed both along and across the gas flow to obtain the most thermally efficient arrangement. The Otahuhu B layout in Figure 1.2 contains 14 heat exchangers in total. The Preheater warms the water before a multi-stage pump sets up the IP and HP pressure levels, and it also acts as economiser for the LP evaporator. A recirculation loop sends part of the preheater outlet water back to its inlet so that exhaust gas leaving the preheater stays above the dew point; below it, acids in the gas condense and corrode the Preheater tubes and HRSG surfaces. HP turbine exhaust is mixed with steam from the second IP superheater and passed to the Reheater before the IP turbine.

Figure 1.2 caption: a simplified diagram of how the Otahuhu B HRSG heat exchangers are arranged. LP, IP and HP mark the low, intermediate and high pressure circuits, and each heat exchanger's role is given by a four-letter code: economiser (ECON), evaporator (EVAP), superheater (SHTR), preheater (PHTR) and reheater (RHTR). Where a pressure level has more than one stage of the same heat exchanger type, a number distinguishes them.

Each HRSG heat exchanger is a bundle of vertically oriented tubes set out in rows in a staggered pattern (Figure 1.3). Compared with an in-line layout, the staggered pattern gives better convective heat transfer through more gas turbulence and mixing [39, 54], but also a larger pressure drop across the bundle, which harms gas turbine performance. Exhaust gas passes over the outer tube surfaces while water enters from the opposite end and travels up and down the tube rows in cross-flow toward the gas inlet. Although water and gas are perpendicular within any single row, the net flow direction opposes the gas, so the arrangement is called counter cross-flow [9].

Figure 1.3 caption: HRSG heat exchanger with staggered tube topology; crosses denote flow into the page and dots flow out of it. Pt is the transverse and Pl the longitudinal tube pitch (spacing), both in m; Nt the number of tubes per row, Nr the number of rows and Nrpp the number of rows per pass of the fluid.

Fins, i.e. extended surfaces, are fitted to the outside of the tubes to raise heat transfer between the fluids, because gases have a comparatively lower convective heat transfer coefficient than liquids [33]. The Otahuhu B HRSG tubes carry segmented (or serrated) fins (Figure 1.4), which add surface area and increase turbulence and mixing in the exhaust gas, improving heat transfer, again at the cost of a higher bundle pressure drop. Figure 1.4 caption: sketch showing a segmented fin tube in cross-section and from above, where di is the inner and do the outer tube diameter, tw the tube wall thickness, df the fin diameter, lf the fin length, tf the fin thickness, ws the segment width and sf the fin spacing, all in meters.

Heat exchangers are usually modelled with either the logarithmic mean temperature (LMTD) method or the effectiveness-NTU (ε-NTU) method. Chapter 3 treats them fully, but their basic equations are restated here; they link fluid properties and heat exchanger construction to the heat transferred, and despite looking different they are effectively equivalent and yield the same answer.

Equation (1.1), LMTD method: Q̇ = UA∆T_LMTD, with ∆T_LMTD = (∆T_1 − ∆T_2)/ln(∆T_1/∆T_2) (heat transferred = overall heat transfer coefficient × heat transfer area × log mean temperature difference). Q̇ is the heat transferred, ∆T_1 and ∆T_2 are the terminal temperature differences between the two fluids, ∆T_LMTD is the mean temperature difference between the fluids over their passage through the heat exchanger, U is the overall heat transfer coefficient and A the area available for heat transfer [27].

Equation (1.2), ε-NTU method: ε = Q̇_actual/Q̇_max; NTU = UA/C_min; ε = f(NTU) (effectiveness = actual heat transfer / maximum possible heat transfer; number of transfer units = UA / minimum heat capacity rate; effectiveness is a function of NTU). Q̇_max is the largest possible heat transfer, Q̇_actual the heat transfer the heat exchanger actually achieves, C_min the minimum heat capacity rate of the fluid and NTU the number of transfer units. ε depends on NTU and the fluid properties, and the relations between them are tabulated in heat transfer textbooks such as [27, 44, 67].

Equations (1.3)-(1.5): U ≈ 1/h_i + 1/h_o (as printed; relates U to the inner and outer fluid heat transfer coefficients h_i and h_o; equation number (1.4) is printed on a blank line), and h = C Re^n Pr^m (heat transfer coefficient expressed as a semi-empirical function of the Reynolds and Prandtl numbers). U depends on how the heat exchanger is built and on fluid properties, and the Chapter 2 review identifies two competing ways of obtaining it. The first computes U from semi-empirical correlations developed for the particular heat transfer application, in which Re and Pr are dimensionless groups depending on fluid properties and duct geometry and C, n and m are constants found by experiment; the thesis calls this the Correlation heat exchanger model.

Equation (1.6): U = U_design (ṁ/ṁ_design)^x (overall heat transfer coefficient = design value × (mass flow / design mass flow) raised to the power x). In this second approach a nominal U, normally the design value, is multiplied by weights formed from the ratio of fluid properties (frequently mass flow ṁ) at the conditions of interest to nominal properties, raised to a power x that is a constant chosen for the specific heat transfer problem; this is designated the Weighted heat exchanger model. The last option assumes U stays at its design value, U = U_design, which is easily found from design fluid conditions using Equation 1.1 or 1.2; this is the Basic heat exchanger model. The three methods form three fidelity levels, the Correlation model being most complex, then Weighted, then Basic.

The goal is to identify which level of model fidelity best suits the simulation of how heat exchangers perform inside a heat recovery steam generator, with particular attention to where the overall heat transfer coefficient comes from and how the way it is determined influences heat exchanger model performance. The work is organised in four steps: (1) build a steady-state heat exchanger model using the three methods of Section 1.3 for predicting the overall heat transfer coefficient; (2) construct a steady-state model of the Otahuhu B CCGT HRSG that incorporates these heat exchanger models; (3) check the model outputs against measured plant data; and (4) compare the performance and accuracy of the various heat exchanger models.

After this introductory chapter with its background material, Chapter 2 surveys literature on simulating CCGT plant operation and on the heat exchanger modelling approaches used in such simulations, motivating these models and revealing the gap concerning which methods best suit heat exchangers in this application. Chapter 3 lays the theoretical foundation of the heat exchanger model from established principles, which leads to the need for the overall heat transfer coefficient, and details three literature methods applied to the Otahuhu B HRSG heat exchangers.

Chapter 4 presents the software environment, then covers the heat exchanger software model's architecture, solution strategy and performance, and the development of the Otahuhu B simulation with its issues, solutions and approximations. Chapter 5 reports case studies simulating the Otahuhu B steam cycle at four points across its operating range with each of the three heat exchanger models, and validates them against existing plant data. Chapter 6 reviews the simulation outcomes, compares the three models, recommends the most suitable one for this application and discusses future research opportunities.

Modelling supports the design, development and operation of industrial processes, which arise from the interplay of many equipment items. Analysing such a process means solving the heat and material balance of the whole system along with sizing and costing equipment, an activity called process flowsheeting [56, 64]. A flowsheet can involve many, even thousands of, equations, and they may need repeated solution, for instance when exploring design alternatives or when recycle streams or nonlinear equations exist. Hand solution soon becomes tedious and error prone, or impossible for large systems, so computer programs were written to build and solve flowsheets; work began in the 1950's with programs that solved only single unit operations, and by the 1970's industry had accepted general purpose flowsheeting programs as standard tools [42, 64].

A modern flowsheeting program has four main parts: a library of unit operations representing each equipment item; a physical properties library for the process materials; numerical methods for solving the equations; and a user interface for specifying the process model. Such programs broadly divide into two categories, sequential modular (SM) and equation oriented (EO) [6, 50].

Most available flowsheeting programs follow the sequential modular approach [37, 50], in which each unit operation is a module bundling its model equations, solution method and user interface; given suitable inputs, it solves its model and returns results. A flowsheeting package offers a library of unit operations for commonly encountered equipment, and specialised packages add domain-specific ones. Unit operations can be linked in any way, outputs to inputs, to represent the whole process.

If unit operations form a linear chain, then with their parameters and any feed streams specified they can be solved one after another, each output feeding the next [50]. Often, however, material or energy generated downstream is returned to an earlier unit, forming recycle streams whose values are unknown at first. Stream tearing guesses these values (the streams are said to be torn) so the system can be solved sequentially, replacing the guess with the newly computed recycle value on each iteration until the recycle values converge sufficiently [37, 64, 50]. This is termed the outer iteration loop, as opposed to inner iteration loop(s) within unit operations that themselves need iterative solution.

Advantages of the sequential modular approach: solution methods are written specifically for one unit operation's equations, giving efficient, robust solution and detailed, specific error messages if a unit fails, and each unit operation can have a tailored user interface that helps correct parameter specification. Disadvantages: finding a solution can be slow, because most processes contain recycle streams and iteratively solved unit operations, and the physical property models are probably iterative too, producing several nested loops. Even with efficient algorithms for properties and units, the absence of analytic derivatives at flowsheet level restricts the solvers available; the outer loop must either use finite difference derivatives, which adds model evaluations and solution time, or successive substitution with tearing of recycle streams [50].

In the equation oriented approach every equation of the process model is collected into one system of equations (SOE) that is solved simultaneously. The user defines the flowsheet much as in SM, choosing unit operations and their connections through the graphical interface, but each unit operation supplies only its model equations. These, plus equations for the interconnections, are assembled into one large SNLE (system of nonlinear equations); the user must give enough information to leave a square, non-singular system, after which the unknowns are initialised and the system solved simultaneously with a multi-dimensional root solver [6, 37, 64, 50].

Holding the whole model in one SOE opens possibilities unavailable to SM. Since the software handles the solution, it can pick algorithms suited to the structure and type of the equations, and a user-defined unit operation needs only its model equations, which can be written in a declarative rather than procedural language, making custom units easier to add than in SM. The equations are expressed in symbolic math notation, letting the software carry out complex operations on the SOE such as obtaining analytical derivatives for the Jacobian [6, 46, 50, 56], which is much faster than numerical derivatives and helps both optimisation and root solving [50]. Solving the SOE is far more efficient than SM, particularly with recycle streams, which sit inside the single SOE and add no extra iteration loops.

Although apparently simpler and more elegant than sequential modular, the EO approach has been hard to implement because of complex software architecture and the algorithms needed for large linear, nonlinear and/or differential equation systems [56], so few commercial products exist. Its chief weakness relative to SM has been solver robustness, especially initialisation [6, 50]: root solvers nearly all rely on Newton's method, which is only locally convergent, so initial guesses must lie near the solution [64]. In SM, small nonlinear systems of single unit operations get case-by-case custom algorithms that supply good guesses, which EO generally cannot do.

Commercial EO programs tackle initialisation in two ways. ASPEN PLUS first solves the system sequentially modularly and uses those results as initial guesses for the equation oriented model [3]. gPROMS instead solves a series of progressively more complex models for each unit operation, the first needing little or no initialisation and each supplying guesses for the next until the intended model is solved, under control of flowsheet-level algorithms; the converged steady-state result can then initialise dynamic simulation, sensitivity analysis, optimisation and so on without repeating the whole solution [18, 50].

Process models may also be steady-state or dynamic. A steady-state model describes the process at one moment, whereas a dynamic model follows behaviour over time, in effect repeating the steady-state solution at many time steps within an interval. Dynamic models serve start-up and shutdown analysis, design of control systems and process training simulators [48]; steady-state models are simpler and faster to solve. The study is confined to steady-state models, justified because a CCGT station usually moves quickly from one steady state to another, a property that makes such stations useful as peaking power plants.

Process modelling software, once used mainly for designing and developing industrial processes, now spans the full lifecycle from concept testing through design, development and operation. In operation, analyses may be offline, with simulations run apart from the plant, or online, with a direct data link between plant and software; Pantelides et al. [49] review the state of process modelling software in plant operation. Being at the forefront of efficient thermal generation, CCGT stations have been the subject of several such studies. Offline work mostly targets optimisation of energy systems including economics: Barigozzi et al. [4, 5] built a THERMOFLEX model of the steam cycle at a northern Italian waste-to-energy plant and used the model data in a MATLAB optimisation to find the best cooling system operating parameters, and Pieve & Salvadori [52] modelled an air-cooled steam condenser at another waste-to-energy plant to choose the optimal number of cooling units for given environmental conditions.

In online operation the model runs beside the real plant on measured data from the plant information system, staying continuously updated and synchronised. It then serves as a performance benchmark: differences between predictions and plant behaviour can signal equipment degradation, which once quantified can enter analyses so maintenance is scheduled by economic benefit rather than operating hours. Commercial plant performance monitoring packages use this arrangement, and installations at CCGT stations have been reported.

Kim & Joo [35] describe deploying the commercial EfficiencyMap monitoring software at two Korean CCGT stations, Seoincheon and Sinincheon. It merges plant model outputs with real-time data to analyse performance, and adds tools for judging gas turbine compressor condition for maintenance scheduling and for optimal load allocation in multi-train (several gas turbine/boiler units) layouts. Plant condition is tracked by correcting current performance to reference load and ambient conditions, so the corrected value should change only with the physical condition of equipment. In a case study of gas turbine power output before and after an overhaul, the system showed an immediate rise of about 4.5 MW, confirmed by plant measurements, demonstrating that it can detect changes in equipment condition.

De Bobadilla et al. [13] report use of the 'EtaPRO' on-line performance monitoring system supplied by General Physic Corporation and installed at Mexico's Naco Nogales combined cycle plant, whose functions resemble those of EFFICIENCYMAP. Monitoring data were used to evaluate changes to the heat rejection system configuration, stopping fans and circulation pumps at low loads and observing the performance response, and heat rate improvements of up to 0.2% were seen.

Heat exchangers are central to CCGT operation, and the reviewed studies model them in various ways; the wider literature allows some generalisation. Among studies that explain their model development in detail, nearly all use the LMTD or effectiveness-NTU (ε-NTU) method for heat transfer. They differ in how the overall heat transfer coefficient U is found. Together with the heat transfer surface area A, U measures how well a heat exchanger transfers heat between two fluids; it was introduced in Section 1.2.1, is covered in Chapter 3, and changes with fluid conditions and heat exchanger geometry. Because U is so central to heat transfer, the way it is determined as fluid conditions change should strongly affect heat exchanger model accuracy. The review covered process modelling and its use in operating CCGT/Cogeneration stations: offline, such software has found optimal operating parameters, and online it has enabled accurate performance monitoring, efficiency gains and potentially better maintenance scheduling. It also revealed two competing, widely used methods for the overall heat transfer coefficient in process models, raising two questions: does variation of U with fluid conditions significantly affect heat exchanger operation, and if so, which method is best for CCGT station modelling? The thesis addresses both by determining the appropriate model fidelity for HRSG heat exchanger simulation, developing three heat exchanger models, embedding them in an Otahuhu B HRSG model and comparing the simulations against measured plant data to judge each method's performance and accuracy.

paragraphs.section: 3 Development of the Theoretical Heat Exchanger Model
paragraphs.text: The chapter builds the theoretical heat exchanger model, starting from a heat and mass balance over the exchanger and then presenting the LMTD (logarithmic mean temperature difference) and ε-NTU (effectiveness - number of transfer units) methods as two usual routes to the thermal energy exchanged between the fluids. Both assume constant isobaric specific heat capacities, and the consequences and possible remedies are discussed. Methods for finding the overall heat transfer coefficient are the core of the study: three approaches are covered, with specific solutions for the exchangers in the Otahuhu B HRSG.

Heat exchangers can be classed by the relative flow directions of the two fluids (Figure 3.1). In parallel-flow both fluids enter on the same side and travel the same way to the outlet; in counter-flow they enter at opposite ends and travel in opposite directions. In cross-flow one fluid runs inside tubes while the other, usually a gas, passes over the tubes at right angles to the internal flow. The development concentrates on the counter-flow exchanger while showing how to adapt the model to parallel and cross-flow. Figure 3.1 caption: representative temperature profiles of parallel flow and counter flow heat exchangers.

Equations (3.1)-(3.2): Q̇ = ṁ_h c_p,h (T_h,inlet − T_h,outlet) and Q̇ = ṁ_c c_p,c (T_c,outlet − T_c,inlet) (heat lost by the hot fluid and heat gained by the cold fluid, each = mass flow × isobaric specific heat × temperature change). Here ṁ is mass flow in kg/s, c_p isobaric specific heat capacity in kJ/kg·K, T temperature in Kelvin (K) and Q̇ heat transfer in kW, with subscripts c and h for cold and hot fluids. These balances assume constant c_p, whose validity depends on the fluid, the temperature change and above all on whether a phase change happens (Section 3.1.4). Neglecting losses to the surroundings, Q̇ is equal for both fluids, the hot fluid's lost energy passing to the cold fluid. Q̇ depends on fluid temperatures and physical construction, and two common ways to link them are the LMTD and ε-NTU methods.

Equations (3.3)-(3.4): Q̇ = UA ∆T (heat transfer rate across a temperature difference = overall heat transfer coefficient × area × temperature difference) and ∆T_LMTD = (∆T_1 − ∆T_2)/ln(∆T_1/∆T_2) (logarithmic mean of the terminal temperature differences). U is in kW/m^2·K, A in m^2 and ∆T in K; the product UA represents the thermal conductance of both fluids and the dividing wall, and its determination, the focus of the study, is treated in Section 3.2. Since fluid temperatures, and hence ∆T, change through the exchanger, the governing differential equations are integrated from inlet to outlet [44, 67] to obtain one representative driving force, the logarithmic mean temperature difference (LMTD).

Equations (3.5)-(3.8), terminal temperature differences: parallel flow ∆T_1 = T_h,inlet − T_c,inlet and ∆T_2 = T_h,outlet − T_c,outlet (inlet-end and outlet-end differences); counter flow ∆T_1 = T_h,inlet − T_c,outlet and ∆T_2 = T_h,outlet − T_c,inlet (hot inlet vs cold outlet, hot outlet vs cold inlet). Counter-flow yields a larger ∆T_LMTD because the temperature difference along the exchanger is higher overall, so it outperforms a parallel-flow unit of equal size, and most heat exchangers are therefore designed counter-flow [33]. Cross-flow units follow suit: fluids cross at right angles in each pass but over several passes usually move counter to one another, a hybrid called counter cross-flow.

Equation (3.9): Q̇ = UA ∆T_LMTD F_corr (heat transfer = UA × LMTD × correction factor for geometry). Substituting the LMTD into Equation 3.3 gives this form, where F_corr corrects for geometries other than pure parallel-flow or counter-flow. F_corr is read from curves for particular exchanger types such as cross-flow and shell and tube in heat transfer and heat exchanger textbooks, e.g. [67] and [33]; for numerical work, fitted equations to these curves exist in the literature, and [62] gives a general approximation whose coefficients are chosen per exchanger type. Equations 3.1, 3.2 and 3.9 together form a system of non-linear equations (SNLE) that is the core of the heat exchanger model.

A heat exchanger model is usually solved either to design an exchanger meeting specifications (the sizing problem) or to find how a given design performs (the rating problem) [33]; the case decides what information is known, which unknowns are sought and so how the SNLE is solved. Sizing seeks UA for a set of design operating conditions, typically inlet temperature, pressure and mass flow of both fluids; one more variable, often one fluid's outlet temperature fixed by the wider system's design requirements, is specified to square the system, which can then be solved directly for the UA needed.

Because the study simulates existing heat exchangers, inlet properties may again be given, but the construction is fixed and UA comes from design data; the aim is to compute Q̇ and from it the outlet fluid properties, which makes solving the SNLE iterative. Software non-linear solvers can handle such systems but need good initial guesses. For the input set T_h,inlet, P_h,inlet, ṁ_h, T_c,inlet, P_c,inlet, ṁ_c and UA, the effectiveness-NTU method gives a direct solution, described next.

The effectiveness-NTU method, an alternative to LMTD, originated with W. M. Kays and A. L. London, who described it in their seminal book Compact Heat Exchangers [34]. It rests on three dimensionless quantities, effectiveness ε, heat capacity rate ratio C_r and number of transfer units NTU, whose interrelation depends on exchanger type and is available as design curves or equations for a limited set of configurations. Equations (3.10)-(3.14): ε = Q̇_actual/Q̇_max (effectiveness = actual / maximum possible heat transfer); Q̇_max = C_min (T_h,inlet − T_c,inlet) (maximum heat transfer = minimum heat capacity rate × largest temperature difference); C_min = min(C_h, C_c); C_h = ṁ_h c_p,h; C_c = ṁ_c c_p,c (heat capacity rate = mass flow × specific heat). C_h and C_c measure each fluid's ability to absorb or reject heat, and Q̇_max is set by the largest temperature difference and limited by the smaller heat capacity rate.

Equations (3.15)-(3.17): NTU = UA/C_min (number of transfer units = UA / minimum heat capacity rate); C_r = C_min/C_max (heat capacity rate ratio); C_max = max(C_h, C_c). Since NTU is proportional to UA, a higher NTU means more heat transfer area and a larger exchanger. By definition C_r ≤ 1, and for a phase change C_r → 0 as C_max → ∞. Table 3.1 gives the effectiveness relation for pure counter-flow and for one fluid changing phase, the latter valid for every flow arrangement, and Table 3.2 inverts these for NTU in terms of ε and C_r. Relations and design curves for other common types, e.g. parallel, single pass cross-flow or shell and tube, appear in textbooks [67, 44, 33, 34], and more complex arrangements are covered in the literature, e.g. Cabezas-Gómez et al. [9] derive ε-NTU relations for multi-pass cross-flow exchangers with complex flow patterns.

Table 3.1 (Effectiveness relation for pure counter-flow heat exchangers and during a phase change (C_r = 0)): Counter-flow: effectiveness relation = ε = {1 − exp[−NTU(1 − C_r)]}/{1 − C_r exp[−NTU(1 − C_r)]} for C_r < 1, and ε = NTU/(1 + NTU) for C_r = 1; All heat exchangers with C_r = 0: effectiveness relation = ε = 1 − exp(−NTU). Table 3.2 (NTU relation for pure counter-flow heat exchangers and during a phase change (C_r = 0)): Counter-flow: NTU relation = NTU = ln[(1 − εC_r)/(1 − ε)]/(1 − C_r) for C_r < 1, and NTU = ε/(1 − ε) for C_r = 1; All heat exchangers with C_r = 0: NTU relation = NTU = −ln(1 − ε). (Effectiveness as a function of NTU and C_r, and its inverse.)

LMTD and effectiveness-NTU both take c_p as constant for each fluid, acceptable for small temperature changes but potentially a significant error for large changes or phase change [44]. Accuracy can be raised by dividing the exchanger into segments (Figure 3.2), each evaluated with properties at its local average temperature, so that any desired accuracy is reached with enough segments. During phase change there is no sensible heating or cooling, so to capture latent heat the balance must be written in enthalpy i rather than temperature. Equations (3.18)-(3.19): Q̇ = ṁ_h (i_h,inlet − i_h,outlet) and Q̇ = ṁ_c (i_c,outlet − i_c,inlet) (heat = mass flow × enthalpy change of each fluid). Figure 3.2 caption: discretised heat exchanger.

Simulating an existing exchanger requires UA. The simplest route solves Equation 3.9 at design operating conditions; with UA and both fluids' inlet conditions known, the outlet states follow. This treats UA as constant, yet U depends on fluid enthalpy and pressure, so when inlet conditions change U departs from its design value. The section details two methods for capturing how U varies with fluid properties.

R_t is total thermal resistance in K/kW; R_i, R_o convection resistances in K/kW; R_f,i, R_f,o fouling resistances in K/kW; R_factor,i, R_factor,o fouling factors in m^2·K/kW; h_i, h_o heat transfer coefficients in kW/m^2·K; A is surface area (m^2), d diameter (m), L tube length (m) and k the tube material's thermal conductivity (kW/m·K); subscripts o and i denote outer and inner surface.

Equations (3.22)-(3.24): 1/U_o = 1/h_o + R_factor,o + A_o ln(d_o/d_i)/(2πLk) + (A_o/A_i) R_factor,i + (A_o/A_i)(1/h_i) (overall coefficient based on outside area); 1/U_i = (A_i/A_o)(1/h_o) + (A_i/A_o) R_factor,o + A_i ln(d_o/d_i)/(2πLk) + R_factor,i + 1/h_i (based on inside area); 1/UA = 1/(U_o A_o) = 1/(U_i A_i) (the total thermal resistance is the same whichever reference area is used). The overall heat transfer coefficient may thus be referred to either the outer or the inner heat transfer surface.

Equations (3.25)-(3.26): 1/UA = R_t = 1/(η_o h_o A_o) + R_factor,o/(η_o A_o) + ln(d_o/d_i)/(2πLk) + R_factor,i/(η_i A_i) + 1/(η_i h_i A_i) (resistance sum including surface efficiency on each side), and for a finned surface η = 1 − (A_f/A_t)(1 − η_f) (overall surface efficiency from fin efficiency and fin-to-total area ratio). Where surfaces carry heat transfer enhancements such as fins, an overall surface efficiency η is applied to that surface; η_f is fin efficiency, A_f fin surface area in m^2 and A_t combined fin plus exposed tube area in m^2. Fin efficiency depends on fin type: simple geometries are covered in textbooks [44, 33] and complex ones in research literature. Fins are common on gas-side surfaces because gases have low convective heat transfer coefficients.

Thermal resistances slow heat flow between fluids at different temperatures. R_wall, the conductive resistance of the tube wall, comes from integrating Fourier's law between inner and outer wall radii [27], with conductivity k depending on tube material and temperature; the Otahuhu B HRSG tubes are carbon steel, with k quoted as 29-55 kW/m·K [27] according to temperature and carbon content. Fouling resistance R_f arises from deposits that insulate heat transfer surfaces [33], quantified by the fouling factor R_factor; typical values from the Tubular Exchanger Manufacturer Association (TEMA) standards let designers ensure required performance in the fouled state between cleans, and in performance modelling typical factors can represent accumulated fouling. In the HRSG, outer-surface fouling is chiefly deposited combustion products (soot/ash), while inner-surface fouling is scale and sludge from the circulating water; Tables 3.3 and 3.4 list typical factors for natural gas flue gas and boiler feedwater.

Per Equation 3.25, the fluids' convective resistances depend on h_i and h_o, which depend on exchanger type and fluid properties. For practical geometries these coefficients generally cannot be derived from first principles, so correlations linking them to fluid properties and configuration have been produced by fitting theoretical forms to measured data. The following two sections give the correlations used for the inner and outer convection coefficients of the HRSG exchangers.

Inside the tubes, water can be single phase liquid or vapour or a two-phase mixture during transition, and the phase strongly affects both heat transfer coefficient and pressure drop, so the model must identify the phase in each segment and apply the matching correlations. For single-phase fully developed turbulent flow in smooth tubes, one of the best known simple correlations is Dittus-Boelter [27]. Equation (3.27): Nu = 0.023 Re^0.8 Pr^n, valid for 0.5 < Pr < 2000 and 2300 < Re < 10^4, with n = 0.4 when the fluid is heated and n = 0.3 when cooled (Nusselt number from Reynolds and Prandtl numbers). Re, Pr and Nu are dimensionless groups of system properties each describing an aspect of the flow.

Equations (3.28)-(3.31): Re = u_avg d/ν = ρ u_avg d/µ = Gd/µ (Reynolds number from velocity, diameter and viscosity, or from mass flux); ν = µ/ρ (kinematic viscosity = dynamic viscosity / density); ṁ = ρ u_avg A_csa (mass flow = density × average velocity × cross-sectional area); G = ṁ/A_csa (mass flux). u_avg is the mean fluid velocity in m/s, d the hydraulic diameter (tube inner diameter) in m, ρ density in kg/m^3, ν kinematic viscosity in m^2/s, µ dynamic viscosity in Pa·s, G mass flux in kg/m^2·s and A_csa pipe cross-sectional area in m^2. Re expresses the ratio of inertial to viscous forces [67] and indicates the flow regime, low values laminar and high values turbulent; the critical pipe value is usually 2300, though transition to fully developed turbulence may span 2000 to 4000 [27].

Equations (3.32)-(3.33): Pr = ν/α = µ c_p/k (Prandtl number = momentum diffusivity / thermal diffusivity) and Nu = hd/k (Nusselt number = convective heat transfer relative to conduction). Pr reflects the relative thickness of the velocity and thermal boundary layers near a surface [67], linked to the fluid's capacity to transport momentum or energy [44]: the more readily a fluid diffuses momentum or energy, the thicker the corresponding boundary layer. α is thermal diffusivity, in the same units as kinematic viscosity. Nu measures how much convection enhances heat transfer above pure conduction (no fluid motion, Nu = 1) [67]; here d is the hydraulic diameter (tube inner diameter) in m, k the fluid thermal conductivity in kW/m·K and h the desired heat transfer coefficient in kW/m^2·K.

Equations (3.34)-(3.35): Petukhov & Kirillov Nu = (f_D/8) Re Pr / [1.07 + 12.7 (f_D/8)^1/2 (Pr^2/3 − 1)], valid for 10^4 < Re < 10^6 with 6 % accuracy for 0.5 < Pr < 200 and 10 % accuracy for 0.5 < Pr < 2000; Gnielinski (1976) Nu = (f_D/8)(Re − 1000) Pr / [1 + 12.7 (f_D/8)^1/2 (Pr^2/3 − 1)], valid for 0.5 < Pr < 2000 and 2300 < Re < 10^4 (Nusselt number for turbulent internal flow from friction factor, Re and Pr). Dittus-Boelter is simple but may err by up to ±25 % [27], so the more accurate Petukhov & Kirillov correlation [51], recommended in [27, 33], is preferred; Gnielinski modified it in 1976 to fit low Reynolds number data better [23].

Friction factor, Equations (3.36)-(3.38): f_d = 64/Re (Hagen-Poiseuille friction factor for fully developed laminar flow, Re ≤ 2300) [44, 27, 65, 11]; f_D = (0.790 ln(Re) − 1.64)^−2 (Petukhov friction factor for turbulent flow in a smooth duct) [51]; 1/√f_D = −2 log[(ǫ/d)/3.7 + 2.51/(Re √f_D)] (Colebrook-White equation including relative surface roughness). f_D is the Darcy friction factor, four times the Fanning friction factor f_F, and depends on the flow regime. Pipe surface roughness, written ǫ as the roughness height in meters above the surface, can strongly affect friction [65], and Colebrook-White is the standard design formula for it. Moody plotted it in 1944 to create the chart named after him [65], showing friction factor versus Reynolds number and relative roughness (ǫ/d). Because it is implicit in f_D it needs iteration, and several explicit approximations exist.

Equation (3.39), Zigrang-Sylvester [69], recommended by Nellis & Klein [44]: 1/√f_D = −2 log{ǫ/(3.7d) − (5.02/Re) log[ǫ/(3.7d) − (5.02/Re) log(ǫ/(3.7d) + 13/Re)]}, valid for 4 × 10^3 ≤ Re ≤ 10^8 and 4 × 10^−5 ≤ ǫ/d ≤ 5 × 10^−2 (explicit approximation of the Colebrook-White friction factor).

Many authors have reviewed explicit friction factor equations, always against Colebrook-White. Zigrang & Sylvester [70] (1985) and Jarić et al. [32] (2011) each judged the Zigrang-Sylvester equation the most accurate surveyed. Winning & Coole [66] (2013) rated many equations on computational efficiency and accuracy versus Colebrook-White, ranking Sonnad & Goudar (2006) [60] best overall; Zigrang-Sylvester was more accurate (mean percentage error 0.019 versus 0.174) but less efficient computationally. Asker et al. [2] (2014) found Sonnad & Goudar (2008) [24] most accurate. Whereas these studies singled out a few very accurate forms, Brkić [8] concluded that, bar a few exceptions, most available equations are acceptably accurate for practical purposes; moreover Colebrook-White, though the accepted standard, is itself only an approximation of measured data, so it may be better or worse than the equations judged against it. Zigrang-Sylvester was chosen chiefly because it is well established, relevant since 1982 and present in reference material, so its behaviour has probably been studied more thoroughly than newer equations.

For two-phase heat transfer, only boiling inside the evaporator must be handled. Nellis & Klein [44] recommend Shah's 1982 internal flow boiling correlation [57], since it was checked against a large experimental database with mean deviation below 20 % and is valid for annular flow and for vertical and horizontal pipes, vertical pipes being relevant here. In [58] Shah compared six widely accepted flow boiling correlations, including his 1982 one, with extensive data on 28 fluids such as water, refrigerants, hydrocarbons and several gases, and the Shah 1982 correlation proved the most accurate and consistent. It is given in Appendix A.

Internal pressure drop model, Equation (3.40): ∆P = f_D (L/d)(ρ u_m^2/2) (Darcy-Weisbach: pressure drop = friction factor × length/diameter × dynamic pressure). ∆P is in Pa; f_D comes from Equation 3.36 for laminar flow (Re < 2300) and Equation 3.39 for turbulent flow. Because the Otahuhu B HRSG evaporators run on natural circulation, their internal pressure drop is taken as zero, so no two-phase boiling friction factor relation is needed. A simplified off-design overall heat transfer coefficient is obtained by dividing the heat transfer correlations at off-design conditions by those at design, which cancels quantities unaffected by fluid conditions and leaves ratios of off-design to design-point fluid properties raised to powers. Erbes & Gay [19] took this approach in models used to simulate a CCGT station at its design point and off it, and HYSYS uses a similar idea in its Weighted heat exchanger model [30]. The equations below, which the text also refers to as the Scaled heat exchanger model (i.e. the Weighted model), come from [19].

Several simplifications lead to an off-design overall heat transfer coefficient equation (denoted U_des in the text). The gas side heat transfer coefficient is far smaller than the water side one and limits heat transfer, so U is governed by gas side conditions and water side effects can be neglected. Equations (3.41)-(3.43): Nu = C Re^x Pr^y (general turbulent heat transfer correlation with constants C, x, y fitted to the fluid and flow) [27, 21]; U/U_des = Nu/Nu_des = (Re/Re_des)^x (Pr/Pr_des)^y (ratio of off-design to design values); and, since for a gas viscosity, Prandtl number and thermal conductivity vary weakly with temperature and can be removed [19], U/U_des = (ṁ/ṁ_des)^x (overall coefficient scales with mass flow ratio to the power x). Erbes & Gay [19] used x = 0.805 for 40 × 10^3 < Re < 400 × 10^3, the value given in [27] for a cylinder in cross-flow.

Gas-side pressure drop uses a simplified correlation from Holman [27]. Equations (3.44)-(3.46): ∆P = (2 f G_max^2 N/ρ)(µ_w/µ_b)^0.14 (bundle pressure drop from friction factor, maximum mass velocity and row count); f = K Re_max^−0.16 (Jakob friction factor) [27]; ∆P/∆P_des = (ṁ/ṁ_des)^1.84 (µ_des/µ)^−0.16 (ρ_des/ρ) (off-design to design pressure drop ratio). G_max is the maximum mass velocity referred to the open frontal area of the HRSG duct left by the tube bank, N counts the longitudinal tube rows, and µ_w and µ_b the dynamic viscosities at wall and bulk (average) temperature. Erbes & Gay [19] note that gas viscosity changes little with temperature and the ratio carries a small exponent, so that factor is effectively constant and dropped. Re_max is the Reynolds number based on G_max and K a tube-bundle geometry factor, constant between design and off-design and therefore cancelled.

Equations (3.47)-(3.49): P = ρ R_gas T (perfect gas law); R_gas = R/M_gas (specific gas constant = universal gas constant / molar mass); ∆P/∆P_des = (ṁ/ṁ_des)^1.84 (T/T_des)(P/P_des)^−1 (gas-side pressure drop ratio expressed in mass flow, temperature and pressure). To avoid evaluating fluid properties, gas µ is assumed to depend mainly on temperature and, from the perfect gas law, ρ is proportional to pressure. Here R denotes the universal gas constant (8.314 J/mol·K) while M_gas is the gas molar mass in kg/mol.

Water-side pressure drop is predicted by dividing the Darcy-Weisbach equation (Equation 3.40) at off-design conditions by the same equation at design, using the simple Blasius friction factor. Equations (3.50)-(3.52): f_D = 0.046 Re^−0.2 (Blasius); ∆P/∆P_des = (ṁ/ṁ_des)^1.8 (µ/µ_des)^0.2 (ρ_des/ρ); and, taking µ as mainly temperature dependent and ρ as pressure dependent, ∆P/∆P_des = (ṁ/ṁ_des)^1.8 (T/T_des)(p/p_des)^−1 (water-side pressure drop ratio). The author remarks that liquid viscosity falls as temperature rises, and since liquids are essentially incompressible it is odd for density to be tied to pressure in this form; for a gas the reverse holds, viscosity rising with temperature and density depending strongly on pressure.

The chapter set out the theory of the heat exchanger model and the ways of computing the off-design overall heat transfer coefficient. Heat transfer can be modelled with the LMTD or ε-NTU method, both of which assume constant isobaric specific heat over the exchanger; this is reasonable for single-phase flow with moderate temperature change but can cause large errors for big temperature changes or phase change, so discretising the exchanger into segments with properties evaluated at each segment's local temperature was proposed.

With both fluids' inlet properties and UA or Q̇ known, ε-NTU solves the exchanger directly, but in a discretised counter-flow exchanger only the end segments have specified inputs; inputs to the other segments must be guessed and iterated, so ε-NTU loses its direct solution. Dumont & Heyen [17] found that LMTD can converge faster than ε-NTU, and LMTD is widespread in commercial thermodynamic software such as HYSYS [30] and VMGsim [25], so LMTD was adopted as the basis of the heat exchanger model.

For the Correlation based exchanger, heat transfer and pressure drop equations for the gas (external) and water (internal) sides were reviewed and the most suitable chosen: ESCOA correlations on the gas side, and on the water side Gnielinski 1976 for single-phase heat transfer, with friction factor from Hagen-Poiseuille for laminar and Zigrang-Sylvester (1982) for turbulent flow. The Weighted model adopts the simplified off-design U method of Erbes & Gay [19]. Its water-side liquid pressure drop equation wrongly assumes dynamic viscosity and density proportional to temperature and pressure, yet Erbes & Gay matched plant performance within 1 % with these simplified equations [19], so they are used unchanged. The next chapter covers software implementation and the practical issues of making the models robust.

Having established the theory in Chapter 3, this chapter explains its software implementation. It first covers the development environment and supporting packages, then the heat exchanger model architecture from the high-level view down to the solution algorithm, then validation of the models against an available analogue, followed by discussion of the results and of any modifications the models required.

The model was written in MATLAB [40]. A high-level scripting language allows fast development and testing, helped by a large library of built-in functions and numerical solvers; it can be extended with user-defined classes and toolboxes, and supports modern practices such as Object Oriented Programming (OOP), unit-testing and built-in git source control. A toolbox is a set of related functions and classes extending MATLAB, and the model relies on two third-party toolboxes: JSteam [38] for fluid property packages and a unit operation library, and OPTI [12] for non-linear equation solvers.

JSteam, from Inverse Problem Ltd., is a utility system and thermodynamic modelling package whose function library is reachable through several interfaces, including as a MATLAB toolbox. It supplies water property routines based on the IAPWS Industrial 1997 Formulation [28] and routines for many pure-fluid and mixture components based on NIST REFPROP [45], plus a library of utility-system unit operations such as turbines and pumps. OPTI is a free optimisation toolbox from the Industrial Information and Control Centre (I^2C^2); for this project its relevant feature is its solvers for systems of non-linear equations, which offer alternatives to MATLAB's standard solvers so that performance can be compared and the best one chosen per application.

Following the sequential modular approach, the model had to be self-contained in data storage and solution algorithm, with three broad requirements: store, analyse and manipulate user input; once the input specification is consistent, build and solve the heat exchanger equation system; and store the results for display or for other connected unit operations. The aim was heat exchanger models of the HRSG economisers, evaporators and superheaters using three ways of evaluating the overall heat transfer coefficient, all sharing the LMTD equations evaluated over any number of segments. An object-oriented design, with each model a specialisation of a minimal base heat exchanger class, met these needs best.

Figure 4.1 (caption: class diagram of the base heat exchanger model) shows the class hierarchy. At the top is UnitOperation, which contains UnitConversion, holding methods and data for unit conversion, and DataStore, a structure that keeps a variable's name, value and related information together for the containing class. UnitOperation is the superclass of all others and provides fluid property calculation, unit conversion, data storage and error reporting. The Stream class stores and handles a process stream attached to the exchanger and can evaluate fluid properties given composition, pressure and at least one of temperature, enthalpy, entropy or vapour fraction.

HeatExchangerSide models one side through which a fluid passes; it holds two Stream objects for inlet and outlet ports and chiefly stores and evaluates property arrays (property profiles) from discretising the exchanger into segments. HeatExchanger implements the base model with two HeatExchangerSide objects and their ports; since commonly one fluid passes over tubes and the other inside them, these are called the shell and tube sides. It directly manages exchanger-level data such as UA and ∆T_LMTD and their profiles, and exposes an interface to its own and contained data so it can track which values the user entered and which were calculated; its solve method runs the solution algorithm (Section 4.2.2). Economiser, evaporator and superheater models are subclasses of HeatExchanger, each slightly altering the solve method so the algorithm can use knowledge of the exchanger type when forming an initial guess. The design and correlation based models are also HeatExchanger subclasses, modified to implement their own solution methods.

Whatever the model, the solution follows the same pattern: check that the user input specification contains enough information to solve; compute an initial guess; hand the non-linear equation solver a function evaluating the heat exchanger equations for the current specification together with the initial guess; and, once the solver converges, store the results and finish.

Equations (4.1)-(4.10), heat exchanger system of nonlinear equations: 0 = ṁ_shell (i_shell,in − i_shell,out) − Q̇ (shell-side energy balance); 0 = ṁ_tube (i_tube,out − i_tube,in) − Q̇ (tube-side energy balance); 0 = UA ∆T_LMTD − Q̇ (rate equation); for counter-flow ∆T_LMTD = (∆T_1 − ∆T_2)/ln(∆T_1/∆T_2) with ∆T_1 = T_shell,in − T_tube,out and ∆T_2 = T_shell,out − T_tube,in; and each temperature is a function of enthalpy and pressure, T_shell,in = f(i_shell,in, P_shell,in), T_shell,out = f(i_shell,out, P_shell,out), T_tube,in = f(i_tube,in, P_tube,in), T_tube,out = f(i_tube,out, P_tube,out) (fluid property calls).

The non-linear solvers are based on Newton's method: from an initial guess x_0, the function is linearised about that point and set to zero to find where it crosses the x-axis; if the guess was close enough this point is nearer the true solution, and repeating with x_0 = x drives x arbitrarily close to it [7]. The hardest part is reliably finding a good initial guess, since a poor one may stop Newton's method converging. The model obtains its guess in two stages: first solving the exchanger as one segment, then interpolating those values for each segment of the discretised exchanger. The single-segment method depends on the input specification and on whether phase change occurs.

Equation (4.11): ∆T_AMTD = (∆T_1 + ∆T_2)/2 (arithmetic mean temperature difference). With no phase change, assumed initially, the AMTD replaces ∆T_LMTD; with c_p held constant at the specified fluid temperature the system becomes linear and can be solved directly. The approximation improves as ∆T_1 and ∆T_2 approach each other, and when ∆T_1 = ∆T_2 the LMTD is undefined while the AMTD is the exact mean difference. Being linear, the AMTD approach is also fast compared with the methods below. To stay linear, however, it must use temperatures rather than enthalpy in the heat and mass balances, so any phase change is ignored and the guess would be poor; when a phase change is detected another method is needed, chosen according to the input specification.

If the specification lets the heat transfer Q̇ be bounded, the bisection method is used: it needs two values x_1 and x_2 bracketing the root of f(x) = 0 so that sign(f(x_1)) ≠ sign(f(x_2)), and repeatedly halves the interval, keeping the half that still brackets the root [7]. For example, with inlet temperatures, pressures, mass flows and UA given, Q̇_max occurs at maximum ∆T_LMTD, when T_shell,in = T_shell,out and T_tube,in = T_tube,out, and the minimum when T_shell,out = T_tube,in and T_tube,out = T_shell,in, where ∆T_LMTD = 0 so Q̇_min = 0. Equations (4.12)-(4.16): bisection seeks Q̇ satisfying 0 = UA ∆T_LMTD − Q̇, with i_shell,out = i_shell,in − Q̇/ṁ_shell, i_tube,out = i_tube,in + Q̇/ṁ_tube, T_shell,out = f(i_shell,out, P_shell,out) and T_tube,out = f(i_tube,out, P_tube,out), and ∆T_LMTD from Equation 3.4 (outlet enthalpies and temperatures computed from a trial heat duty).

Bisection is guaranteed to converge if the root lies within the bounds and the function is continuous, but convergence is slow (linear), so once close enough a Newton based method can finish the job. The model implements bisection with the MATLAB function fzero, which also uses the secant method for superlinear convergence without needing the derivative. Bisection only applies when the root can be bracketed; for instance, with only the hot fluid outlet temperature given there is no evident upper bound on its inlet temperature.

The alternative technique is homotopy: the equation system is modified into a form with an easily found consistent initial guess, then returned step by step to its original form, re-solving with Newton's method at each step so the guess is always near the solution and convergence is fast and robust. If both fluids have mass flow plus either inlet or outlet temperature and pressure fixed, along with UA, then UA can first be set to zero so that heat transfer is zero and the unknown temperatures equal the specified ones; UA is then raised in increments, each solution (initially zero heat transfer) seeding the next, until UA reaches its specified value. Homotopy is robust but very slow and is a last resort; it is implemented with the arc length continuation method of [7].

After the initial guess, the exchanger is split into the required segments. For the base model, heat transfer and pressure drop are assumed uniform per segment; because each side's mass flow is fixed, the enthalpy profile is divided evenly, and all other quantities follow from enthalpy and pressure profiles: temperature profile, then each segment's ∆T_LMTD, then each segment's UA. The design and correlation based models must compute UA before this guess procedure: the design based exchanger starts from UA_design and ∆P_design, while the correlation based exchanger assumes no temperature change on either side so the correlations can be solved for initial UA and pressure drop.

Three solvers are available for the non-linear system: fsolve [40], HYBRJ [12] and MKLTRNLS [12]. fsolve, built into MATLAB, is Newton-Raphson based and picks the Newton step with the trust region dogleg algorithm. HYBRJ is an open source MINPACK solver based on the Powell Hybrid method [53]; without an analytic Jacobian it obtains the initial Jacobian matrix by finite differences and then uses Broyden's rank-1 Jacobian update, cutting function evaluations and speeding solution. MKLTRNLS, from the Intel Math Kernel Library [31], is a non-linear least squares solver that can solve an SNLE by fitting it to the zero vector 0. HYBRJ and MKLTRNLS are accessed in MATLAB through the OPTI toolbox.

Which solver is best depends on the problem. fsolve compares well when given an analytic Jacobian in sparse form; otherwise HYBRJ is faster but frequently less robust. MKLTRNLS usually needs fewer iterations than fsolve but is slower when an analytic Jacobian exists, as it does not exploit sparsity. The base heat exchanger's equations are simple enough for an analytic Jacobian, whereas for the Weighted and Correlation models analytic derivatives are harder to obtain and the solvers use a finite-difference approximation.

All validation runs used one segment per exchanger, matching how GTPro simulates individual heat exchangers for a fairer comparison, but every model can divide an exchanger into any number of segments to evaluate properties at each segment's local temperature, as Figure 4.4 shows for the evaporator case (caption: evaporator temperature profiles of each model when 10 segments are used). In normal HRSG operation each exchanger handles water in only one state, liquid, two-phase or vapour, so extra segments matter little for the Basic and Weighted models. They do matter for the Correlation model's tube side heat transfer coefficient in the evaporator, which varies greatly as water goes from subcooled liquid to saturated vapour (Figure 4.5).

Figure 4.5 caption: how the tube side convective heat transfer coefficient changes while water is heated from subcooled liquid through to superheated vapour. The abrupt changes in that curve mark laminar-to-turbulent transitions and switches between the Petukhov-Kirillov and Gnielinski correlations as Re changes. Within the Shah flow boiling correlation, the liquid-fraction part of the coefficient comes from the single-phase correlation; as vapour fraction rises, liquid content and hence liquid Reynolds number fall, so near the top of the curve the method shifts from Petukhov-Kirillov to Gnielinski once Re drops below 1×10^4. Evaluated as one segment, the Correlation exchanger would use the mean of inlet and outlet enthalpies and obtain 35–40 kW/m^2·K instead of the correct average 18.1 kW/m^2·K.

The added accuracy costs solution time (Figure 4.6, caption: solution time of each heat exchanger model as the segment count grows). The Basic model's time stays roughly constant, the Weighted model's grows from 0.0329 to 1.0783 s, and the Correlation model's rises most steeply, reaching 35.006 s with 20 segments compared with 0.5252 with one. This is tolerable for single exchangers, but inside a larger iteratively solved process model the nested loops can make solution times extremely long.

Equation (4.17): (10 s × 14 × (1 + 17) × 10)(1 hr/3600 s) = 7 hr (solution time = time per exchanger × number of exchangers × (1 + unknowns) evaluations per iteration × iterations). Example: the Otahuhu B HRSG model of the next chapter has 14 counter-flow exchangers and 17 unknowns (14 exhaust gas outlet temperatures, one per exchanger, and three feed water mass flows for LP, IP and HP). A 10-segment Correlation model takes about 10 s per solution (Figure 4.6), and each solver iteration needs one model evaluation plus one per unknown for the finite-difference Jacobian; at 10 iterations the HRSG would take 7 hr. To keep the accuracy while cutting time, the Correlation model was modified so that tube side heat transfer coefficient and pressure drop are evaluated on 10 segments, averaged, and then used to solve the exchanger as a single segment.

Validation also showed that the Shah flow boiling correlation gave wrong values at low Reynolds numbers (Re < 1000), traced to the Petukhov-Kirillov and Gnielinski correlations used inside the Shah routine; these were replaced there by the simpler Dittus-Boelter correlation (Figure 4.7). The lower accuracy of the boiling coefficient is of little concern because it is much larger than the single-phase or shell side coefficients, and the smaller coefficients tend to dominate the overall heat transfer coefficient. The chapter presented the development environment, supporting software and model implementation, and its issues. Because several related heat exchanger models were needed, an object-oriented architecture was used, improving code reuse and maintenance and easing changes, which sped development. The hardest challenge was reliably finding good initial guesses for the Newton based solvers; no single approach was best, so several methods were implemented for different input specifications and fluid conditions. Validation against GTPro economiser and evaporator test cases showed all models closely matching the GTPro economiser temperature profiles, except the Correlation model's tube side pressure drop of 0.2770 bar versus 0.3292 bar. For the evaporator, the Weighted and Correlation models gave UA of 170.73 and 177.30 against GTPro's 201.55 kW/K, yet their temperature profiles and tube side mass flows still agreed closely with GTPro.

The heat exchanger models are assembled into a model of the Otahuhu B HRSG. Since no measurements exist for the gas turbine exhaust mass flow entering the HRSG, an off-design gas turbine model is built to estimate it at part load. The combined models then simulate the HRSG at four points across the station's operating range, and the results are compared with plant data to judge each heat exchanger model.

In a CCGT station the gas turbine exhaust is the heat source driving the steam cycle through the HRSG, so although the study targets the HRSG heat exchangers, HRSG operation is tightly coupled to the gas turbine and the exhaust gas properties at given operating conditions must be known. The manufacturer's published data for the Otahuhu B gas turbine refer to nominal load under ISO conditions, namely 15 °C, 1.013 bar and 60 % relative humidity, i.e. the design point at maximum power output, also called base or full load. These nominal values shift with ambient conditions and load, so a gas turbine model is developed to predict part-load behaviour as a function of ambient temperature, pressure and required load.

A gas turbine has three main parts, compressor, combustion chamber and turbine (Figure 5.1, caption: gas turbine process flow diagram). Here turbine, compressor and generator share one shaft, typical of large industrial power generation gas turbines [55]. Ambient air at point 1 is drawn into the compressor, which raises its pressure and temperature, leaving at point 2; it is then mixed with natural gas and burned in the combustion chamber. Combustion products at point 3 reach about 1200 − 1400 °C in modern machines [36], the turbine inlet (or firing) temperature (TIT), which together with compressor pressure ratio (PR) largely sets cycle performance. The products expand through the turbine, whose work drives the compressor with the surplus generating electricity; the turbine exhaust temperature (TET) at point 4 still exceeds 500 °C [68], and the HRSG recovers most of the remaining heat.

Each component is modelled separately via a steady-state heat and mass balance over its control volume, and the components are combined to represent the whole gas turbine; compressor and turbine are treated as isentropic with an efficiency applied for real-process irreversibilities [68]. Equations (5.1)-(5.2): compressor η_comp = (i_2,isen − i_1)/(i_2 − i_1) with ṁ_1 = ṁ_2 (isentropic over actual enthalpy rise); turbine η_turb = (i_3 − i_4)/(i_3 − i_4,isen) with ṁ_3 = ṁ_4 (actual over isentropic enthalpy drop).

Equations (5.3)-(5.6): T_3/T_2 = [1 + η_b FAR (LHV/c_p) T_2]/(1 + FAR) (combustor outlet to inlet temperature ratio); FAR = [(T_3/T_2) − 1]/[η_b (LHV/c_p) T_2 − (T_3/T_2)] (fuel air ratio needed for a given temperature rise); FAR = ṁ_fuel/ṁ_air (fuel air ratio definition); η_gt = (W_turb − W_comp)/(ṁ_fuel LHV) (gas turbine efficiency = net work / fuel energy rate) [26]. In the combustion chamber, fuel mass flow, lower heating value (LHV) and combustion efficiency η_b give the energy released, and the equations can be solved for outlet temperature T_3 or for fuel or air mass flow. Given suitable inputs for an operating point, Equations 5.1 to 5.6 fully describe the gas turbine, a typical input set being Table 5.1. This model yields mass flows from inputs but cannot properly predict how behaviour changes with load and ambient conditions; that part-load (off-design) modelling follows.

Table 5.1 (Basic gas turbine model input parameters), input (unit) → output (unit): Tamb (°C) → ṁfuel (kg/s); Pamb (bar) → ṁair (kg/s); Texhaust (°C) → ṁexhaust (kg/s); further inputs without output pairing: PR, ηcomp, ηgt, Net power (kW), Fuel LHV (kJ/kg).

Given the Table 5.1 inputs, sourced from the manufacturer or assumed typical nominal values, the basic model yields air, fuel and, crucially, exhaust gas mass flows. The gas turbine is designed for, and is most efficient at, these nominal conditions, but plants must often run away from them to follow dispatch orders from the power system operator (citation printed as [?]), which lowers performance; these effects must be modelled for accurate off-design predictions. That requires knowing the control methodology and component off-design behaviour [26, 37]. Combined cycle gas turbines are controlled by inlet guide vanes (IGV) and fuel throttling: the IGV, a set of stationary vanes at the compressor inlet, when closed cuts air flow through compressor and turbine, lowering turbine work and output, while the firing temperature rises, so fuel flow must also fall to keep TET acceptable.

Reducing compressor air flow lowers compressor pressure ratio and efficiency and hence cycle efficiency η_gt; turbine efficiency is also affected, but compressor effects dominate off-design behaviour, so turbine changes are neglected [37]. Compressor off-design characteristics are often captured with compressor maps [36, 55], plots linking efficiency, pressure ratio, mass flow and temperature over the operating range, or with manufacturer correction curves [37] giving percentage changes in design values versus off-design conditions such as ambient temperature. Both are specific to a gas turbine model and were unavailable for Otahuhu B, so equations from [37] predicting compressor off-design mass flow and efficiency from design data and current conditions are used instead, offering a simple approximation that fits readily into the existing gas turbine model.

Equations (5.7)-(5.9): ṁ_air = ṁ_air,des (P_1/P_1,des)(T_1,des/T_1)(1 − (∆IGV)(VFC))[1 + TFC((T_1 − T_1,des)/T_1,des)] (off-design air mass flow from inlet pressure, inlet temperature and IGV change); η_comp = η_comp,des (1 − FC|(ṁ_air − ṁ_air,des)/ṁ_air,des|)[1 + SEC|(n − n_max)/n_max|] (off-design compressor efficiency from mass flow and speed deviation); (ṁ_3,des √T_3,des)/P_3,des = (ṁ_3 √T_3)/P_3 (choked turbine inlet flow function held constant). VFC denotes the vane flow, TFC the temperature flow, FC the mass flow and SEC the compressor speed efficiency correction factor; ∆IGV is the IGV angle change from design and n compressor speed, with design speed usable for n_max.

Equation 5.7 gives off-design air flow from design values (subscript des) plus current compressor inlet temperature, pressure and IGV change, and Equation 5.8 uses it to compute off-design compressor efficiency; for power generation the speed is fixed at 3000 rpm (50 Hz), so the speed term is zero. The correction factors can be tuned to a particular machine. Equation 5.9 assumes the turbine inlet stays choked at design and off-design, needed because no turbine characteristic curves were available; the largest departure is at low load, where compressor pressure ratio may be over-predicted, but normal operation uses only part of the range, where the turbine first stage inlet nozzle is usually choked or close to it [37, 55].

Part-load solution procedure: design data first fix design-point compressor, combustion and turbine efficiencies plus fuel mass flow and TIT, which are passed to the off-design model. Off-design it is most useful to solve for a fixed load rather than a fixed ∆IGV, making ∆IGV an unknown. Guesses are made for ∆IGV and PR; Equations 5.7 and 5.8 give off-design air flow and compressor efficiency; Equation 5.1 gives compressor outlet enthalpy i_2; since TET stays roughly at its maximum design value, the turbine is solved for whatever TIT keeps it there, which yields fuel mass flow; Equation 5.9 gives turbine inlet pressure. The guessed PR and the required load are compared with computed values, and if they differ new ∆IGV and PR guesses start the next iteration.

Measured plant values of compressor efficiency, pressure ratio, gas turbine efficiency and fuel mass flow were used to validate the procedure (Figure 5.2). Exhaust mass flow is not measured, but it is assumed that if these key intermediate values match the plant, the predicted exhaust flow is similarly accurate. Equation (5.10): η_pump = (i_outlet,isen − i_inlet)/(i_outlet − i_inlet) and Ẇ_pump = ṁ_inlet (i_outlet − i_inlet) (pump isentropic efficiency and pump work from enthalpy rise). IP and HP streams next enter the first stage economisers, which share a tube bundle side by side across the gas flow, taking roughly 1/4 and 3/4 of the exhaust gas mass flow respectively, so in the model the gas path is divided so both see the same gas inlet temperature and pressure, and recombines the paths at the gas outlet with a heat and mass balance, averaging the two outlet pressures.

Equation (5.11): i_outlet = (ṁ_inlet,1 i_inlet,1 + ṁ_inlet,2 i_inlet,2)/(ṁ_inlet,1 + ṁ_inlet,2) and ṁ_outlet = ṁ_inlet,1 + ṁ_inlet,2 (mixer outlet enthalpy as mass-weighted average; outlet flow as sum). The two gas paths join in a mixer unit operation (Figure 5.5, caption: mixer unit operation symbol). Several other exchangers also share tube bundles and occupy only part of the duct width; they lie roughly in sequence along the gas path but receive only a fraction of the total gas flow. These fractions, derived from design data and listed in Table 5.3, are held constant over the operating range and multiplied by total exhaust flow to give each exchanger's gas flow.

The HRSG model was run for four case studies spanning Otahuhu B's operating range: 222, 265, 326 and 382 MW. Although rated at 400 MW, the plant's highest output in the data is about 380 MW, and the 222 MW minimum corresponds to the gas turbine IGV nearing its minimum angle. Cases were picked with similar ambient conditions and close in time to limit effects of changing plant condition such as fouling. Predictions are compared with plant data at several points in plots whose upper panel shows predicted and measured values at the four load points and lower panel the absolute percentage error for each heat exchanger model.

Figure 5.6 (caption: Preheater and LP superheater 2 outlet temperatures compared). Predicted Preheater outlet temperature is off by roughly 10 °C at full load down to 5 °C at minimum load; since all models agree, the error may stem from a wrong value in the HRSG model, possibly a constant error in measured recirculation flow. For LP superheater 2 steam outlet, the off-design (Weighted and Correlation) models track plant data within 1.5 %. The Basic model agrees at 382 MW but falls faster as load drops: its fixed overall heat transfer coefficient keeps heat transfer relatively high at low load, removing more energy from the gas early in the HRSG and lowering gas inlet temperatures downstream, which reduces downstream heat transfer and water/steam outlet temperatures. Because of this reduced transfer, the initial gas temperature deficit is damped by successive exchangers until, as at the Preheater outlet, it is barely noticeable.
