The Weighted model follows plant data across the load range within 2 %. The Correlation model sits well below, fairly consistently, from about 10 °C at maximum load to 15 °C at minimum load, because its gas inlet temperature is lower than the Weighted model's. That reduction arises upstream at the HP evaporator, whose predicted UA at maximum load is about 474 kW/K (24 %) above design (Table 5.6), affecting all downstream exchangers. As with the Basic model, cooler gas lowers heat transfer and so the gas temperature change across successive exchangers, so the effect is strongest just after the HP evaporator and the Correlation-Weighted gas temperature gap shrinks below 2 °C at the LP superheater 2 inlet. For the Basic model the cooler gas inlet temperatures show up as a large fall in water/steam outlet temperature with load. Since these exchangers lie further upstream than LP superheater 2, their gas temperature reduction is larger and the drop in water/steam outlet temperature correspondingly big.

Figure 5.8 (caption: outlet temperatures of the Reheater and of the last stage HP Economiser compared) shows Reheater and HP superheater 2 outlet temperatures, which every model predicts to rise as load falls. As explained in Section 5.1, inlet guide vane (IGV) control holds exhaust gas temperature constant as load decreases, strongly influencing HP superheaters 1 and 2, the Reheater and HP evaporator. With gas inlet temperature roughly constant, falling steam flows reduce the steam heat capacity rate, so a given heat transfer causes a bigger temperature rise; for exchangers nearest the gas inlet this outweighs the reductions in heat transfer from lower mass flows, UA and steam inlet temperature, raising steam outlet temperature.

The off-design models agree closely on Reheater outlet temperature but lie about 15 to 20 °C from plant data from maximum to minimum load. The Basic model matches them at maximum load but over-predicts as load falls, because its fixed overall heat transfer coefficient sustains higher heat transfer than the off-design models and the plant. The large gap may come from the HRSG model ignoring desuperheaters at the inlet and outlet of HP superheater 2 and the Reheater, which keep steam within limits for the tubes and steam turbine inlets, as shown by the fairly constant measured outlet temperature over the load range. Fouling-reduced heat transfer may also contribute: per [43], fouling is greatest at the HRSG entrance and lessens as temperature drops and particles are filtered from the gas. HP superheater 2 shows the same trends as the Reheater.

Figure 5.9 (caption: LP and IP evaporator steam mass flows compared) and Figure 5.10 show evaporator steam flows. All models predict LP steam flow close to measurement; the percentage errors look large only because LP flow is small, e.g. the Weighted model's 5.2 % error at maximum load is 0.56 kg/s, and its 5.6 % at minimum load just 0.29 kg/s. The Weighted model's IP steam flow agrees with measurements, while, because the IP evaporator lies upstream of the LP evaporator, the cooler gas affects the Basic and Correlation predictions, which follow the same pattern as the outlet temperatures in Figure 5.7.

Figure 5.10 (caption: HP evaporator and Reheater steam mass flows compared). Every model's HP evaporator gas inlet temperature stays near 450 °C over the load range, so differences in predicted HP flow stem from UA: the Correlation model over-predicts HP evaporator UA, and the Basic model uses a fixed nominal value. Design data put nominal HP steam flow near 75 kg/s; the lower measured value may reflect fouling reducing heat transfer and steam generation, or flow meter inaccuracy. Reheater flow is simply the sum of IP and HP flows and, dominated by the larger HP flow, resembles the HP plot. Despite differing individual predictions, the models' total feed water (LP, IP and HP) flow is about the same.

Figure 5.11 gives HRSG solution times (caption: HRSG model solution times for each heat exchanger method; runs were made in MATLAB 2015b on a 64 bit laptop with an Intel Core i5-4200U CPU, 1.6 GHz). The Correlation model is far slower, about 3600-5000 s, and more variable, from about 5000 s at nominal load to 3600 s at minimum load, since each case is initialised from the previous solution and a better initial guess speeds and stabilises convergence. The Basic and Weighted models take roughly 200 and 370 s, nearly unchanged across cases.

Ideally predictions would match measurements exactly, but the study's main purpose is to compare how well the three heat exchanger models predict part-load behaviour of the HRSG exchangers; parameters can later be tuned to fit nominal-load plant data. The models were therefore judged on predicting changes in behaviour as load falls, not on absolute accuracy.

At most points the Basic model, with fixed overall heat transfer coefficient, fails to track the part-load trends in plant data. This was expected, but the results reveal complex interactions among HRSG exchangers: at reduced load its high UA values increase heat transfer in the exchangers from the gas inlet up to and including the HP evaporator, which extracts the single largest share of exhaust energy. The high UA lowered the gas temperature leaving the HP evaporator by about 23 °C relative to the Weighted model, reducing heat transfer in the following exchangers, and this lower transfer narrowed the Basic-Weighted gas temperature gap towards the stack.

The Weighted model mostly predicted measured data accurately over the load range, with notable exceptions: the outlet temperatures of the Preheater, Reheater and HP superheater 2, and the HP mass flow. The Reheater and HP superheater 2 discrepancies may be explained by the model omitting the desuperheaters at their inlet and outlet that keep steam within equipment limits, or by fouling degradation, which is worst nearest the gas inlet and would affect these exchangers most.

The Correlation model generally captured the right trends but was usually offset. Exchangers downstream of the HP evaporator saw cooler exhaust gas because the HP evaporator UA was over-estimated, and, by the same mechanism as for the Basic model, this produced lower predicted water/steam outlet temperatures further downstream. The Weighted and Correlation models show very similar trends across the load range, and since the Correlation model computes UA from first principles, this further validates the Weighted model's simplified treatment of how the overall heat transfer coefficient varies with load.

With no measured exhaust mass flow, a part-load gas turbine model was built and its parameters hand-tuned so that key quantities such as compressor efficiency and fuel mass flow matched plant data over the operating range, on the assumption that matching these intermediates makes the computed exhaust flow similarly accurate. The chapter described the simulation procedure and analysed the results. The Basic model could not correctly predict load-driven changes in exchanger performance, whereas the Weighted and Correlation models followed the measured trends as load fell. The Correlation model, however, over-estimated HP evaporator UA, sharply lowering exhaust gas temperature early in the HRSG and offsetting downstream predictions from the measurements and the Weighted results.

The study sought the appropriate fidelity for heat exchanger models in simulating existing Combine Cycle Gas Turbine (CCGT) stations ("Combine" as printed). Since most literature and commercial models use the LMTD or ε-NTU method as the accepted standard, the focus was the off-design variation of the overall heat transfer coefficient U. Three literature approaches were identified: hold U at its design value regardless of operating changes, scale U with related fluid properties, or compute U from empirical correlations for the specific problem; these became the Basic, Weighted and Correlation models. They were placed in a model of the Otahuhu B CCGT heat recovery steam generator (HRSG), simulated at four load points covering the plant range, and compared with plant data.

At nominal load the Basic model agreed with plant data as well as the Weighted model did, but its predictions worsened as load fell, as expected given a U fixed for nominal operation. The Weighted model followed plant trends and, at most points, predicted exchanger outlet temperatures and mass flows accurately, except the HP mass flow and the water/steam outlet temperatures of HP superheater 2, the Reheater and the Preheater, possibly due to HRSG model deficiencies that would need further plant information to confirm. The Correlation model generally followed plant trends and the Weighted model's trends but was offset in absolute terms, attributed to an over-predicted U for the early-positioned HP evaporator, whose resulting cooler exhaust gas reduced heat transfer downstream.

Each approach has application-dependent pros and cons. The Basic model is easiest to set up and fastest, and performs well if operation stays close to where U is accurately known. The Weighted model predicts off-design performance relative to a known nominal point, accurate nearby and less so further away; once an accurate nominal point is set, matching real off-design behaviour only needs adjusting three exponents (x, y, z), but it requires a complete nominal operating point specification.

The Correlation model predicts changes in operation about as well as the Weighted model and, by deriving U solely from the physical construction, needs no full nominal data set, though as the results show this does not guarantee accuracy even at the nominal point. Its complexity makes fine tuning to the plant harder, and for real-time simulation its run time matters: every Correlation run took over an hour to converge, during which plant operation could change. Overall the Weighted model is judged the most effective for simulating heat exchangers in existing CCGT stations, matching the plant at nominal point, following off-design changes, being simple to set up and converging in reasonable time.

Several improvements to the models are possible, some omitted for lack of time and others addressing problems met during simulation. The Weighted model could be sped up by implementing analytical derivatives instead of the current finite differences. The Correlation model, the most complex, has the most scope. The LMTD correction factor F_corr adjusts ∆T_LMTD for configurations other than pure counter-flow; Cabezas-Gómez et al. [9] showed counter cross-flow performance approaches pure counter-flow as row count rises, but for four rows, the fewest they studied, effectiveness can differ from pure counter-flow by up to 6.7 %, averaging 1.5 % over the fluid properties considered. Otahuhu B has several exchangers with under four rows, implying larger errors, and the VDI Heat Altas (spelling as printed) [62] gives an equation for F_corr in terms of fluid properties and tube row count that could be added to the Correlation model.

Equations (6.1)-(6.3): (µ_b/µ_w)^n (property-variation correction for liquids based on bulk-to-wall viscosity ratio) [33]; (T_w/T_b)^m (correction for gases based on wall-to-bulk absolute temperature ratio) [33]; Q̇ = hA(T_w − T_b) (convective heat flow used to find wall temperature) [27]. Because fluid properties change with distance from the tube surface, the heat transfer coefficient and friction factor correlations can be multiplied by a correction factor: for liquids viscosity change with temperature indicates the other property variations, while for gases properties vary directly with absolute temperature. Subscripts b and w denote bulk (average) and wall (tube surface) properties, and h is the fluid convective heat transfer coefficient; the procedure is iterative and must sit inside the model's iteration loop.

The HRSG model solves slowly because every heat exchanger model must converge iteratively, one at a time, before each outer-loop iteration of the HRSG solver completes, repeated until the outer loop converges. This is acceptable for the Basic and Weighted models, but the Correlation model took over an hour in every case study, ruling it out for real-time CCGT monitoring. Solution could be accelerated by dropping discrete heat exchanger unit operations and writing the exchanger equations directly into the HRSG model, solving one large non-linear system simultaneously. Drawbacks are greater complexity, harder debugging, model initialisation and possibly less flexibility depending on the software framework [64, 50], but with a suitable framework (Chapter 2) this could be much faster and make correlation-based exchanger models more viable for this application.
